items.excerpt: AI firms including Amazon and Anthropic are buying millions of physical books — many rare or out of print — and destructively scanning them for training corpora. Authors, booksellers and historians object that irreplaceable copies are being pulped purely for their text.

Jane Friedman unpacks how Claude's new text watermark actually works and why critics call it 'compliance theatre': the mark is applied when Claude is used for assistive editing tasks rather than for fully generated text, which inverts what authors and editors need from disclosure.

Patrick Hargitt and Steve Smith argue that AI retrieval tools can locate a paper but rarely know which version they read, and that persistent identifiers alone don't fix it. They call for semantic versioning and provenance metadata baked into publishing workflows so AI-mediated reading stays traceable.

Reedsy's Ricardo Fayet argues AI search engines are rewriting book discoverability: readers now ask conversational questions instead of typing keywords, so books get surfaced by review volume and cross-web mentions rather than metadata keywords. Authors are told to build an 'internet footprint' across Goodreads, Reddit and reviews so LLMs can recommend them.

Elizabeth Ann West and Stacey Anderson preview 'The Ultimate Automated Author Experience,' a big-picture roadmap for an end-to-end AI-assisted authoring stack — drafting, revision and production — coming this fall from Future Fiction Academy.

Book Riot's AI publishing roundup covers Anthropic's Claude watermarking under new EU transparency rules, Substack's rollout of the Pangram detector, and AuthorProof — an app from novelist Vera Kurian that cryptographically records the writing process to prove human authorship instead of relying on AI detection.

Book Riot's library news roundup leads with a study in which readers rated AI-generated stories higher than human-written ones when told they were human-authored, and notes writers now inserting deliberate typos and style quirks to dodge AI detection.

A first look at Story Hacker OS, an AI writing environment that helps novelists build stronger stories using genre templates, trope libraries and a book builder while keeping the author in control of craft decisions — framed as AI making you a better fiction writer, not replacing you.

Self-publishing news roundup on how Europe's new AI transparency rules are reaching authors worldwide through Claude, a study challenging assumptions about AI-generated writing, and a record number of Pulitzer winners and finalists disclosing AI use in their work.

McGraw Hill now runs eight live AI learning tools with 7.5 million active users and three more launching this fiscal year. Its AI Reader — which lets students highlight passages inside an e-book and self-quiz — logged 63 million learning interactions across 2.6 million students since fall 2024.

Ashutosh Ghildiyal proposes a 'cognitive responsibility' framework splitting mechanical cognition (retrieval, pattern-matching) that AI can own from non-mechanical cognition (discovery, discernment, judgment) that humans must keep. He warns editorial and peer-review workflows lose independent judgment when AI mediates direct contact with evidence.

Jason Hamilton traces the shift from chatbots to agentic writing workflows and argues authors who adopt AI as a process tool rather than a text vending machine have little to fear — a practical read on where publishing tooling is heading.

Episode 49 of The Automated Author argues the biggest shift in AI fiction writing is context, not prompts: the same model gives one author great prose and another randomness depending on the systems, story knowledge and skills built around it.

The UK trade is debating whether authors of colour are disproportionately accused of using generative AI, after a run of online speculation targeting several debut and mid-list writers. Agents call the pattern 'hard to ignore' as unverifiable AI allegations become a reputational weapon.
